newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Russian capital flees economic chaos - much illegally.
newsitem.headline: Russian capital flees economic chaos - much illegally.

text.p: The Russian economy has lost up to $60 billion in capital flight because of political and economic instability and high taxes, a senior analyst said on Thursday.

Sergei Shibayev, partner in the international accountancy firm Coopers & Lybrand, told a conference on money laundering in Central and Eastern Europe that some studies put Russian capital flight as high as $100 billion but that the central bank had given licences for some $800 million to go abroad.
This meant that much of the capital flight was illegal.

"If you have high taxes or instability, and that is the main reason for capital flight in Russia, you have the same problem," Shibayev told the conference, which brough together bankers, regulators and law enforcement officials to discuss harmonising measures to tackle money laundering.
The Russian economy is mired in a deep payments crisis. Many companies do not pay suppliers or receive payment for goods and services. In turn they do not pay wages or taxes.
At the same time, many areas of the economy have been deeply infiltrated by structures with links to organised crime. Shibayev said organised crime controlled some 41,000 companies and many banks.
"The major thing is the stabilisation of the whole situation in Russia. Without this you are just attacking the symptoms, not the root causes of the problem," Shibayev said.
He said a commonly-used means of transferring money abroad was by pre-payment to a foreign company for goods and services which were never delivered.
Common destinations for the money included Switzerland, Cyprus, Germany and Britain but cash was also kept closer to hand in, for example, Hungary or the Baltic States.
Shibayev said detailed data of capital flight in most other Eastern European countries was not available.

But John Taylor, general counsel for the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), said money laundering could be partially behind the collapse of pyramid schemes in Albania which have sparked sometimes violent unrest in Europe's poorest state.
"Money laundering in all its manifestations is an activity that will harm sound market economies and good business practice," Taylor told the conference.
David Bickford, a senior consultant for British-based Inter Access Risk Management, said the total "global criminal product" was some $1 trillion of which some 70 percent was drug-related.
All of this had to be laundered and in many cases, Western financial intermediaries would be used.

"The best option for the international community is to harmonise its approach to defeat organised crime," said Bickford, a former legal adviser to British intelligence services, who said more regulation of money wire transfers was among likely steps.

Rowan Bosworth-Davies of law firm Titmuss Sainer Dechert said U.S. law meant institutions involved in transferring suspect money were liable to prosecution if any part of the transaction involved U.S. companies or markets.
